entry.title: The anti-lexicographic SUS-anchor: a near-optimal k=1 sampling scheme
entry.summary:
Table of Contents 1 Abstract 2 Introduction 3 Preliminaries
3.1 Minimizers and sampling schemes 3.2 Bidirectional string anchors 3.3 Maximal suffixes 4 Character-based orders 5 Smallest unique substring anchors
5.1 Properties 5.2 Computing SUS-anchors 6 Results 7 Discussion \[ \newcommand{\sus}{\mathsf{SUS}} \newcommand{\lcp}{\mathsf{lcp}} \newcommand{\last}{\mathsf{last}} \] 1 Abstract
Link to heading
Motivation. In recent years, there has been a renewed interest in the search for low density minimizer schemes. These schemes take a window of \(w\) consecutive \(k\)-mers, and sample one of them: the smallest under some specific order. Schemes such as the mod-minimizer provide a low density (fraction of sampled \(k\)-mers) when \(k \gg w\), while schemes such as the greedy minimizer work well for explicit small parameters roughly in the regime \(k \leq 2w\), for \(k\) and \(w\) up to \(15\) or so.

entry.title: Concurrent, atomic MSI hash tables
entry.summary:
Readers will be familiar with Mask-Step-Index (MSI) hash tables, a technique for building fast, open-addressed hash tables in a dozen lines of code. If multiple threads or processes access an MSI table with at least one still inserting elements, care must be taken to avoid data races. This article will show how to add atomic operations to MSI tables in order to support different concurrency constraints. Let’s begin with the simplest case: An integer hash set, no deletions, only one insert thread (single producer), and consumers do not care about insert order. That is, the producer inserts A then B, but consumers may observe B in the table before A. Suppose this is the hash table in the single-threaded case:

entry.title: Traffic Premonitions
entry.summary: Exactly a year ago, an ambulance in Bangalore hit several people. The next day I was driving my scooter on the road besides an ambulance. The sight of the ambulance reminded me of the news story and I thought to myself, “it could happen to me, I should be careful.” We were stopped at a traffic signal, and I was lost in thoughts about the news. The signal turned green, we started moving, the ambulance took a sharp turn, and ran into me. Thankfully, both of us hit the brakes quite hard and the collision was minor. I got a severe whiplash from the sudden stop, and had to suffer through a backache for the next three months.
